paragraphs: One who wishes to be meticulous should make the windings (kericha) of the tzitzit in segments (chulyot), each segment consisting of three windings. First, one ties two knots close to the corner of the garment, then winds seven windings, then ties two more knots, then winds eight windings, then ties two more knots, then winds eleven windings, then ties two knots, then winds thirteen windings, and afterward ties two more knots. The total sum of all the windings is thirty-nine (39), corresponding to the numerical value of the phrase 'the Lord is One' (HaVaYaH echad). This is as our teacher (the Arizal), of blessed memory, wrote in Sefer HaKavanot. And I made a mnemonic for this matter: 'Give a portion to seven, and also to eight' (Ecclesiastes 11:2) — first come seven windings, then eight windings; then one makes eleven windings, corresponding to the number of letters in the phrase 'to seven, to eight' (lshiv'ah lishmonah), which are eleven letters; and then one makes thirteen windings, corresponding to the number of letters in the phrase 'give a portion to seven and also' (ten chelek l'shiv'ah v'gam), which are thirteen letters.

clarification.explanation: When making the tzitzit in the more meticulous manner ('segment by segment'), they are divided into segments, each made up of three windings. First, two knots are tied close to the corner of the garment, then seven windings are wound, then again two knots, followed by eight windings, again two knots, then eleven windings, again two knots, and finally thirteen windings, after which two final knots are tied. The total sum of all the windings is thirty-nine (39), which corresponds to the numerical value of the phrase 'HaVaYaH echad' (the Lord is One) in gematria. The numbers of windings (7, 8, 11, 13) are not arbitrary: they are hinted at in the verse 'Give a portion to seven, and also to eight' (Ecclesiastes 11:2), which Rabbi Yosef Chaim made into a mnemonic for this matter — seven and eight appear explicitly, the number of letters in the phrase 'to seven, to eight' is eleven, and the number of letters in the phrase 'give a portion to seven and also' is thirteen.
takeaways: The meticulous method: two knots, 7 windings, two knots, 8 windings, two knots, 11 windings, two knots, 13 windings, two knots — a total of 39 windings.
The number of windings at each stage is hinted at in the mnemonic sentence and adds up to the gematria of 'HaVaYaH echad' (the Lord is One).

paragraphs: A gentile who hung the threads of tzitzit on a garment, or who made the segments and knots — it is invalid. But a woman is valid to place the tzitzit on the garment and to make the segments and knots, though there are those who are stringent that it should not be done by women. Therefore, ab initio, one must be careful that the hanging of the threads, their winding, and their tying not be done by women but by men — however, the spinning and twisting of the threads themselves may be done ab initio by women as well. A minor's status in this matter is like that of a woman; therefore, ab initio, the hanging of the threads, the windings, and the knots should not be done by a minor but by an adult. However, anyone who is thirteen years and one day old may do it ab initio, and there is no need to check whether he has grown two hairs.

clarification.explanation: If a gentile is the one who tied the threads of the tzitzit onto the garment, or made the segments and the knots — the tzitzit is invalid and one cannot fulfill the obligation with it. By contrast, a woman is valid according to the basic law to hang the tzitzit on the garment and to make the segments and knots, though some are stringent about this. Therefore, in practice, it is preferable ab initio that the hanging, winding, and tying of the tzitzit threads be done by men rather than by women — but the spinning and twisting of the threads themselves may be done ab initio by women as well. The law of a minor (a child) in this matter is like that of a woman — meaning, it is likewise preferable ab initio to avoid having him do the hanging, winding, and tying, and to prefer an adult instead. But if the minor has reached the age of thirteen years and one day, he may do so ab initio, and there is no need to check whether he has already shown signs of physical maturity ('two hairs').
takeaways: A gentile invalidates the tzitzit entirely if he is the one who hung or tied it.
Ab initio, it is preferable that adult men (from age 13 and one day) perform the hanging of the threads, the winding, and the tying, even though women are valid to do so according to the basic law.

paragraphs: If a Jew hung tzitzit on a garment without intent — meaning he did not intend it for the sake of the mitzvah of tzitzit — there are those who invalidate it and those who validate it, and the halachah follows the opinion of those who invalidate it. Therefore, one must untie them and re-hang them for the sake of the mitzvah of tzitzit. And if it is Shabbat, when it is not possible to untie and retie them, and he has no other valid tallit, one may rely on those who validate it for that day alone; and after Shabbat he should fix it, but should not recite a blessing, since doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency, and blessings do not hold up the fulfillment of the mitzvah. Therefore, every person should be careful to rely, in the hanging of the threads and their preparation, only on a God-fearing person of established reliability who is expert and knows how to have the proper intent for the mitzvah and to do everything correctly. He should therefore be careful to say beforehand, 'I hereby hang these tzitzit for the sake of the mitzvah of tzitzit,' since some say that anything requiring intent for its own sake must have that intent expressed verbally — as the later authorities wrote regarding the law of spinning and twisting. And it is good to say: 'For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, etc. — I am hereby prepared to hang tzitzit on the four corners of this garment, as the Lord our God commanded us in His Torah, "And they shall make for themselves tzitzit on the corners of their garments," and it is stated, "You shall make yourself twisted threads on the four corners of your covering with which you cover yourself." May it be Your will, Lord our God and God of our fathers, that just as we fulfill this mitzvah with white threads, so may You merit us to fulfill it properly with threads of tekhelet, as written in the Torah, "And they shall put upon the tzitzit of each corner a thread of tekhelet," and "May the pleasantness [of the Lord our God be upon us]," etc.'

clarification.explanation: One who hung tzitzit on a garment without explicit intent for the sake of fulfilling the mitzvah of tzitzit — there is a dispute as to whether the tzitzit is valid, and the halachah follows the stringent opinion that it is invalid. Therefore, one must untie the tzitzit and re-hang them with explicit intent for the sake of the mitzvah. In the special case of Shabbat, when it is not possible to untie and retie (due to the prohibitions of Shabbat) and the person has no other valid tallit, it is permitted to be lenient and rely on the lenient opinion for that Shabbat day alone, but one should not recite a blessing over that tallit due to the doubt (since 'doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency' — in a case of doubt, one does not recite a blessing). After Shabbat, one should fix the tzitzit properly. From this the halachic conclusion follows that one must be careful to rely, in the hanging and preparation of the threads, only on a God-fearing and expert person who knows how to have proper intent at the time of hanging, and it is even fitting for him to state explicitly that he is doing this 'for the sake of the mitzvah of tzitzit' (since some say that intent required to be for its own sake must be expressed verbally), and it is also proper to recite a short prayer formula of 'for the sake of unification' along with a request that we merit to fulfill the mitzvah also with threads of tekhelet, as we were commanded in the Torah.
takeaways: Tzitzit that was hung without explicit intent for the mitzvah is invalid according to the halachah, and must be untied and re-hung with intent.
On Shabbat alone, in a case of great need, it is permitted to be lenient and use such a tallit without reciting a blessing over it.
It is recommended to say explicitly, 'I hereby hang these tzitzit for the sake of the mitzvah of tzitzit,' at the time of hanging.

paragraphs: It is good to be careful not to cut the threads of the tzitzit with a knife, following the principle stated, 'You shall not lift up iron upon them,' but rather one should cut them with one's teeth when they need to be cut.

clarification.explanation: It is proper to be careful not to cut the threads of the tzitzit with a knife or an iron implement, but rather to cut them with the teeth when there is a need to do so. The reason for this is based on the principle learned from the altar of the Beit HaMikdash, 'You shall not lift up iron upon them' — refraining from bringing an iron implement (which symbolizes killing and warfare) into contact with things of holiness.
takeaways: It is preferable to cut tzitzit threads with the teeth rather than with a knife or other iron implement, on account of the principle 'You shall not lift up iron upon them.'

paragraphs: If one borrowed a garment with tzitzit: if he borrowed it in order to wear it to go up to the duchan (for the Priestly Blessing) or to be called up to the Torah, and the like, he should not recite a blessing over it. But if he borrowed it in order to fulfill the mitzvah of wrapping oneself in tzitzit — if he borrowed it from the sexton without the owner's knowledge, he should not recite a blessing over it, since blessings do not hold up the fulfillment of the mitzvah, and since there is a dispute, doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency. But if he borrowed it with the owner's knowledge in order to wrap himself in it and fulfill the mitzvah of tzitzit, he may recite a blessing, for we say that presumably it was given to him as a gift on condition that it be returned, and it is thus considered his own. And although even in this case some say that one should not recite a blessing over a borrowed tallit at all, nevertheless in such a case one may rely on the custom, and one should not protest against the one who recites the blessing. However, a God-fearing person should distance himself from a borrowed tallit where possible. And tallitot of consecrated property (hekdesh) that are placed in the synagogue as an act of charity, for the use of those who have no tallit of their own, one should recite a blessing over them according to all opinions, even if one wears them in order to be called up to the Torah, as the later authorities wrote regarding this.

clarification.explanation: One who borrowed a garment with tzitzit: if he borrowed it in order to wear it for going up to the duchan or to the Torah scroll and the like — he should not recite a blessing over it. But if he borrowed it in order to fulfill the mitzvah of wrapping himself in tzitzit: if he borrowed it from the sexton without the owner's knowledge — he should not recite a blessing (since blessings do not hold up the fulfillment of the mitzvah, and since there is a dispute — doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency); but if he borrowed it with the owner's knowledge in order to wrap himself and fulfill the mitzvah — he may recite a blessing, since presumably it was given to him as a gift on condition of return, and it is thus considered his own. And although here too some say that one should not recite a blessing over a borrowed tallit at all — one may rely on the custom and should not protest against the one reciting the blessing; nevertheless, a God-fearing person should distance himself from a borrowed tallit where possible. And tallitot of consecrated property placed in the synagogue as an act of charity, for the wearing of one who has no tallit — a blessing is recited over them according to all opinions, even when worn in order to go up to the Torah scroll (as the later authorities wrote).
takeaways: A borrowed tallit for going up to the duchan or the Torah scroll — no blessing is recited; for the purpose of the mitzvah of wrapping oneself — a blessing is recited only if borrowed with the owner's knowledge.
Some say that no blessing at all should be recited over a borrowed tallit; the custom of reciting the blessing is relied upon, but a God-fearing person should distance himself from it.
Tallitot of consecrated property in the synagogue (charity) — a blessing is recited over them according to all opinions.

paragraphs: In our time we observe that most people are particular that others should not wear their tzitzit and tefillin. Therefore, one should not take from the sexton the tzitzit or tefillin of others without the owners' knowledge, unless the sexton knows with certainty that the owners are not particular about this. And not all opinions are equal in these matters — indeed, I myself recognize that I am among those who are particular about this, and the reasons vary.

clarification.explanation: In our time, most people are particular and do not want others to wear the tzitzit and tefillin that belong to them. Therefore, one should not take from the synagogue sexton the tzitzit or tefillin of another person without his knowledge, unless it is certain to the sexton that that person is not particular about this. And since not everyone is the same in this matter (some are particular and some are not), each person must evaluate his own particular situation, and Rabbi Yosef Chaim himself admits that he himself is among those who are particular about this, for various reasons.
takeaways: One should not take another person's tzitzit or tefillin from the sexton without clear permission from their owner, since many people are particular about this.

paragraphs: It is permitted to untie the tzitzit from a tallit, whether large or small, for the sake of beautifying the mitzvah, in order to put in their place new and more beautiful tzitzit — even though the tzitzit that are removed are simply discarded and put away, and are not placed on another tallit, this is permitted on account of beautifying the mitzvah. Likewise, if one corner has torn and one wishes to renew all four for the sake of appearance, so that they be equal and resemble one another, it is permitted to remove all three other tzitzit and make all four corners new, so that they be equal together, for the sake of beautifying the mitzvah.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to untie old tzitzit from a tallit (whether a large or a small tallit) in order to replace them with new and more beautiful tzitzit, for the sake of beautifying the mitzvah — and this is so even though the tzitzit that are removed are discarded and put away and are not transferred to another tallit, since it is all considered beautification of the mitzvah. Similarly, if one corner of the four corners of the tallit has torn and the person wants all four corners to look uniform and equal, it is permitted to remove the three intact tzitzit and make new tzitzit anew on all four corners together, so that they be uniform and beautiful.
takeaways: It is permitted to replace intact tzitzit with new and more beautiful ones, solely for the sake of beautifying the mitzvah.
If one corner has torn, it is permitted to renew all four corners together so that they be uniform.

paragraphs: Even though the windings of the tzitzit were made to correspond to the number of the name HaVaYaH, since some have this custom and do not follow the custom of thirty-nine windings, it is permitted to untie them, and there is no concern of erasing the [Divine] Name in this, as the later authorities wrote.

clarification.explanation: There are those who have the custom of making the number of windings of the tzitzit correspond to the gematria of the name HaVaYaH (rather than the usual number thirty-nine). One who does not follow this custom of thirty-nine windings and wishes to untie such tzitzit — this is permitted, and there is no concern of 'erasing the [Divine] Name' (the prohibition against erasing God's name) involved, since these windings are not considered an actual writing of God's name that is forbidden to erase.
takeaways: It is permitted to untie tzitzit that were wound to a number corresponding to the gematria of the name HaVaYaH — there is no prohibition of erasing the [Divine] Name involved.

paragraphs: When one wishes to untie the tzitzit in order to put on more beautiful ones, and the effort of untying them is difficult for him, it is permitted to cut them, even though they thereby become completely ruined. However, there are those who are stringent about this and forbid cutting them, and one must be concerned for their words; only in a case of great difficulty and great need may one rely on those who permit it — so concluded the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: One who wishes to untie the tzitzit in order to replace them with more beautiful ones, and finds the effort of undoing the knots difficult — it is permitted for him to cut them, even though they thereby become completely ruined and can no longer be used again. Nevertheless, there are those who are stringent and forbid cutting them, and one must be concerned for their words; only in a case of great difficulty and great need may one rely on the lenient approach.
takeaways: One should untie the tzitzit rather than cut them, out of concern for the opinion of those who forbid it; only in a case of great difficulty and great need — when untying them is very hard — is it permitted to cut them.

paragraphs: A tallit with tzitzit that split into two parts — it is forbidden to sew it back together with the tzitzit that are on it, on account of the principle 'it must be made [for the mitzvah], not the result of something already made.' What should one do? He should untie the tzitzit from specifically one of the two parts, and then sew the parts together, so that this part which has no tzitzit is like an addition to the first part; and afterward he should make new tzitzit on this part, which is [now] an addition to the first — so I concluded in my holy book, Makabtzeil, from the books of the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: A tallit with tzitzit that has torn into two parts — it is forbidden to sew it back together along with the tzitzit that are on it, because of the halachic principle 'it must be made [for the mitzvah], not the result of something already made' (the mitzvah must be performed from the outset, and not result from an action already performed in the past). The solution: one must first untie the tzitzit from only one of the two parts, and then sew the two parts of the tallit together — so that the part from which the tzitzit were removed is considered a new addition to the first part (which still has tzitzit on it). Afterward, one should make new tzitzit on this part, which is now considered an addition to the original tallit.
takeaways: A tallit that has torn in two — it is forbidden to sew it back together with the existing tzitzit, because of 'it must be made, not the result of something already made.'
The solution: untie the tzitzit from one part, sew the parts together, and then make new tzitzit on the part that was added.

paragraphs: The measure of the large tallit is that it should encompass the entire head and the entire body up to the chest, front and back, as our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote in Sefer HaKavanot. And our Sages, of blessed memory, said that it should be enough to cover the head and most of the body of a minor. In my holy book Makabtzeil I brought the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, what he wrote in Sefer HaKavanot, and what is written in Olat Tamid, and what is written in Nahar Shalom by our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, and I compared the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, with the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, for this measure that our Sages, of blessed memory, stated regarding a minor — requiring most of his body — is equivalent to the measure that our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, stated regarding an adult — up to the chest — and he did not state 'most of his body.' And there I raised a doubt: regarding this measure required for an adult, up to the chest — if a very tall person could wear a tallit that reaches, on an average-sized person, up to the chest, even though on him it does not reach up to the chest. And I concluded that we follow the stringent view, such that it must reach up to the chest of the one wearing it, since from the unqualified wording of our teacher the Ari's words, of blessed memory, it appears rather that one must measure each person according to his own stature. However, we do not act leniently in this: if there is a person of very short stature, who is grown in years but whose stature is short, like the measure of a nine-year-old minor, he cannot wear a tallit that reaches him up to the chest, since this tallit does not reach up to the chest of an adult [of ordinary stature].

clarification.explanation: The measure of the large tallit (worn during prayer) is such that it should encompass the entire head and the entire body up to the chest, front and back, as our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote in Sefer HaKavanot. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that the measure is to cover the head and most of the body of a minor. Rabbi Yosef Chaim compares the two measures and discovers that they are in fact identical: what the Sages said regarding a minor (most of his body) is equivalent to what the Ari, of blessed memory, said regarding an adult (up to the chest). Rabbi Yosef Chaim discusses the question: a very tall person — may he wear a tallit that reaches up to the chest of an average-height person, even though relative to his own height it does not reach that far? He concludes that one should be stringent and ensure that the tallit reaches up to the chest relative to the personal height of the wearer, as seems more implied by the unqualified words of the Ari, of blessed memory. However, this is not applied leniently — that is, a person of very short stature, even though he is already an adult in years, cannot wear a tallit fit for the measure of a nine-year-old minor if it does not reach up to the chest according to the measure of a normal adult.
takeaways: A large tallit must cover the head and body up to the chest, front and back.

The measure should be gauged according to the personal height of the wearer — but only for stringency: a person of short stature does not fulfill the obligation with a small tallit, even though it reaches his own chest.

paragraphs: Regarding the measure of the small tallit (tallit katan) worn under one's clothes, in my holy book Makabtzeil I brought the words of the later authorities on this matter, and there I brought what the Gaon Rabbi Chaim Palache, of blessed memory, concluded in Lev Chaim, siman 99, that the proper measure to fulfill one's obligation according to all opinions is to make the small tallit an amah and a half, which is thirty-six gudalim, in length, and an amah and a half in width — all the more so according to the opinion of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, who requires covering the body front and back — until here are his words, see there. And one who examines will see in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, that he did not say regarding the small tallit that it should cover front and back, but rather stated a measure that it should wrap the body aside from the arms; and from this it appears that the width need not be an amah and a half, which is thirty-six gudalim, but regarding the length I concede that he correctly ruled so according to the opinion of the Tur and those who agree with him, that its length must be made an amah and a half, which is thirty-six gudalim. Now, here in our city of Baghdad, may it be built and established, the custom is to make the small tallit an amah and a quarter by the local measure, which comes to more than forty gudalim in length, but the width is made three-quarters of an amah, which comes to more than twenty-four gudalim. And in a responsum to another city I instructed the questioner to make the width twenty-four gudalim and the length thirty-six gudalim.

clarification.explanation: Regarding the measure of the small tallit (worn under one's clothes throughout the day), Rabbi Yosef Chaim brings the opinion of Rabbi Chaim Palache, of blessed memory, that the proper measure to fulfill one's obligation according to all opinions is an amah and a half (36 gudalim) in length and an amah and a half in width, especially according to the approach of the Ari, of blessed memory, which requires covering the body front and back. However, Rabbi Yosef Chaim notes that the Ari, of blessed memory, did not state explicitly that the small tallit must cover front and back, but only that it should wrap the body (aside from the arms) — and therefore there is no necessity that the width be specifically an amah and a half (36 gudalim), though regarding the length he agrees that it is correctly ruled, according to the opinion of the Tur and those who agree with him, that the length must be made an amah and a half (36 gudalim). In the custom of Baghdad, they used to make the small tallit more than forty gudalim in length and about twenty-four gudalim in width, and in a responsum to another city Rabbi Yosef Chaim instructed a width of 24 gudalim and a length of 36 gudalim.
takeaways: The measure of the small tallit ab initio: length of about 36 gudalim (an amah and a half); regarding the width, one may be more lenient than with the length.
The local custom (Baghdad) was longer tallitot, but Rabbi Yosef Chaim ruled elsewhere on 36 by 24 gudalim.

paragraphs: Women and slaves are exempt from the mitzvah of tzitzit — even if they wear a four-cornered garment, they do not need to place tzitzit on it, because it is a positive time-bound commandment, and women and slaves are exempt from every positive time-bound commandment. And although we hold regarding shofar and sukkah and the like that if they wished to fulfill the mitzvah they may, and they receive reward like one who is not commanded but performs the act, and there is no issue of 'one who is exempt from a matter and performs it is called a fool' — nevertheless, regarding this mitzvah [of tzitzit] it appears as haughtiness (yuhara), and there is also a concern of 'a woman shall not wear a man's article.' Therefore, regarding tzitzit one must prevent them, as mentioned in the halachic authorities. And in Sefer HaKavanot a specific reason for this mitzvah is explained, based on the mystical tradition, why this mitzvah does not apply to women.

clarification.explanation: Women and slaves are exempt from the mitzvah of tzitzit — even if they wear a four-cornered garment, they do not need to place tzitzit on it, because it is a positive time-bound commandment, and women and slaves are exempt from every positive time-bound commandment. And although regarding mitzvot such as shofar and sukkah, if they wished to fulfill them, they may do so and receive reward as one who is not commanded but performs the act, without the concern of 'one who is exempt from a matter and performs it is called a fool' — nevertheless, regarding tzitzit specifically, the matter appears as haughtiness (yuhara), and there is also a concern of 'a woman shall not wear a man's article'; therefore, regarding this mitzvah, they should be prevented from doing so (as mentioned in the halachic authorities). And in Sefer HaKavanot a specific reason is explained, based on the mystical tradition, as to why this mitzvah does not apply to women.
takeaways: Women and slaves are exempt from tzitzit — since it is a positive time-bound commandment — even with a four-cornered garment.

Regarding tzitzit specifically, they should be prevented from performing it (it appears as haughtiness, and there is a concern of 'a woman shall not wear a man's article'), and there is also a reason for this based on the mystical tradition.

paragraphs: A minor who knows how to wrap himself [in a tallit] — his father must acquire tzitzit for him to train him in the mitzvah. Regarding this minor, some say [the age is] nine years, and some say: one who is bright is trained from age six, and one who is not bright, from age seven — his father must acquire tzitzit for him to train him.

clarification.explanation: A young child who already knows how to properly wrap himself in a tallit — his father is obligated to buy him tzitzit in order to train him in the mitzvah. There is a dispute as to the exact age: some say from the age of nine years; and some say it depends on the child's sharpness of mind: a bright child (wise and understanding) already at age six, and if he is not so bright — only at age seven, the father must buy him tzitzit to train him in the mitzvah.
takeaways: From age six (if bright) up to nine — the father is obligated to train his son in the mitzvah of tzitzit and buy him a tallit.

paragraphs: Night is not the time for tzitzit, as it is stated, 'and you shall look upon it,' excluding a garment [designated] for the night. But the garment of a blind person is obligated in tzitzit, because he is subject to being seen by others; therefore, even if a blind person wears it, he is obligated to place tzitzit on it. In my holy book Rav Pe'alim I brought, in my responsum there, the words of the Gaon Rabbi Chaim Palache, of blessed memory, in Lev Chaim, siman 100, who wrote that although we hold that a blind person is obligated in tzitzit, nevertheless, since there is one who says that the blind person is exempt, he should fulfill the mitzvah of tzitzit without a blessing, due to the principle that doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency. And there I brought proofs that since the widespread custom is that the blind person does recite the blessing, he should recite the blessing, and there is no need to be concerned about doubtful blessings being omitted as a leniency; and even Rabbi Chaim Palache, of blessed memory, himself wrote likewise in his book Mo'ed LeChol Chai, siman 10, letter 48, that where there is a [prevailing] custom, we do not say 'doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency.' And this is a simple, widespread custom, that the blind person recites the blessing over the tallit. And if he were to come to be pious and hear the blessing from others [instead], this is difficult to do every day, and moreover, this approach raises a further difficulty from another angle.

clarification.explanation: At night there is no obligation of tzitzit, as derived from the verse 'and you shall look upon it' — indicating that the mitzvah depends on seeing, and therefore a garment designated for the night (which is not seen) is exempt from tzitzit. However, the garment of a blind person is indeed obligated in tzitzit, even though he himself cannot see it, because others do see him wearing it — therefore a blind person, too, is obligated to place tzitzit on his garment. Regarding the blessing, there is an opinion (Rabbi Chaim Palache) that since there is one who holds that a blind person is entirely exempt from the mitzvah of tzitzit, it is fitting for the blind person to fulfill the mitzvah without a blessing, out of doubt. But Rabbi Yosef Chaim proves that since the prevailing custom is that blind people do recite the blessing, there is no need for concern over the doubt, because the principle of 'doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency' does not apply where there is a clear custom. And Rabbi Chaim Palache himself wrote likewise elsewhere, that where there is a simple custom, one does not follow the doubt regarding blessings. Rabbi Yosef Chaim adds a further practical reason why one should not refrain from the blessing: one who wishes to be stringent with himself and fulfill the obligation according to all opinions by hearing the blessing from another person — this is difficult to do every single day, since there is not always someone available to recite the blessing on his behalf; and besides this, there is also a further difficulty and hesitation with this approach from another angle. Therefore, in practice, the blind person recites the blessing himself over his tallit as usual, following the simple custom.
takeaways: Tzitzit is not obligatory at night (a night garment is exempt), but the garment of a blind person is obligated in tzitzit because others see him wearing it.
The prevailing custom is that a blind person recites the blessing over the tzitzit — one should follow this and not be concerned about the doubt, especially where there is a clear custom.
A further practical reason: relying on another person's blessing instead of reciting it oneself is difficult to do every day, so it is preferable for the blind person to recite the blessing himself.

paragraphs: Since there is a dispute between the Rambam and the Rosh regarding a garment designated for day and night [both], and Maran, of blessed memory, did not reveal his opinion regarding a garment designated for the night and worn during the day — therefore one must be stringent, as a matter of Torah prohibition, according to the stringencies of both the aforementioned opinions, to place tzitzit on a garment designated for day and night even if worn at night, and likewise one should place tzitzit on a garment designated for the night if worn during the day. But regarding the blessing, since doubtful blessings are omitted as a leniency, one should recite a blessing only when wearing, during the day, a garment designated for the day, or when wearing, during the day, a garment designated for both day and night, as mentioned by the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: There is a dispute between the Rambam and the Rosh regarding a garment designated exclusively for day or for night, and Maran (Rabbi Yosef Karo) did not explicitly decide the question of a garment designated for the night that is worn during the day. Therefore, out of stringency in a matter of Torah law, one must place tzitzit both on a garment designated for day and night even when worn at night, and on a garment designated for night when worn during the day — this way one fulfills the obligation according to both opinions. But regarding the blessing, since there is a doubt, the practice is to be lenient and not recite a blessing except when wearing, during the day, a garment designated for the day (or a garment designated for both).
takeaways: Out of doubt, one should place tzitzit even on a night garment worn during the day, and on a garment designated for both day and night when worn at night.
But a blessing is recited only when wearing, during the day, a garment designated for the day (or for both day and night).

paragraphs: Sheets and pillows, even though a person sometimes sleeps in them during the day, are called 'night garments,' since they were fundamentally made for the night. And according to the one who says that a night garment is obligated in tzitzit if worn during the day, one would need to place tzitzit on them, since one indeed sleeps in them in the morning. Nevertheless, the widespread custom is not to place tzitzit on them, even if they are made of wool, because some say that the Torah obligated only garments that a person covers himself with in the manner of wearing, but items used in the manner of spreading, such as sheets and pillows, are not called a 'garment.' Nonetheless, since there are those who disagree, one should round off one of the four corners of the sheet in order to exempt it according to all opinions. This applies to sheets made of wool; but for cotton, silk, and the like, there is no need to round off a corner, since here there is a compounded doubt (sfek sfeka): perhaps they are exempt by Torah law [entirely], and perhaps the halachah follows the opinion that a garment designated for the night is exempt during the day. And whenever there are two doubts of Torah law, even though rabbinically it would be [treated as] a single doubt, one may rely on this leniently — so wrote the Gaon Eshel Avraham, siman 18, se'if katan 3. And it appears to me that there is here in fact a third doubt: perhaps the halachah follows the opinion that anything used in the manner of spreading and not in the manner of wearing is not called a 'garment' at all and is exempt. Therefore, one need not be particular regarding sheets of other materials; but regarding wool, even though there too there is a compounded doubt, since it is easy to fix by rounding off one corner, one does not rely merely on this compounded doubt in a matter of Torah prohibition.

clarification.explanation: Sheets and pillows, even though a person sometimes sleeps in them during the day too, are considered 'night garments' because they are fundamentally made for use at night. According to the opinion that holds that a night garment is obligated in tzitzit when worn during the day, one would need to place tzitzit on sheets if one sleeps in them in the morning as well. But the widespread custom is not to place tzitzit on them at all, even if they are made of wool, since there is an opinion that the Torah obligated tzitzit only on garments that one actually wears (in the manner of wearing), and not on items used for 'spreading' (laying over the bed) such as sheets and pillows. Nevertheless, since there are those who disagree, it is customary to round off one of the four corners of the sheet, in order to exempt it entirely from the need for tzitzit — but this is done only when the sheet is made of wool; for sheets of cotton, silk, and the like, there is no need even for this. The reason for this: there are two doubts that combine here, as the Gaon Eshel Avraham wrote — (a) perhaps there is no obligation of tzitzit at all on items of 'spreading'; (b) perhaps the halachah follows the opinion that exempts a night garment from tzitzit during the day; and two doubts of Torah law are considered a 'compounded doubt' (sfek sfeka), which is lenient enough even in a matter of Torah prohibition. But Rabbi Yosef Chaim adds, on his own authority, that there is in fact a third doubt specifically regarding fabrics that are not wool: perhaps the halachah follows the opinion that anything done 'in the manner of spreading' and not 'in the manner of wearing' is not called a 'garment' at all and is entirely exempt — and because of these three combined doubts, one need not be particular at all regarding sheets of cotton, silk, and the like. But regarding a wool sheet, which has only the first two doubts (an ordinary compounded doubt), since it is easy to fix by rounding off one corner, one does not rely on the doubt alone in a matter of Torah prohibition, and the correction is actually carried out.
takeaways: The custom: tzitzit is not placed on sheets and pillows, even if made of wool.
For a wool sheet alone, the custom is to round off one of the four corners in order to exempt it entirely from the obligation; for sheets of other fabrics, not even this is necessary.

The reason for the distinction: for non-wool fabric, Rabbi Yosef Chaim has his own additional third doubt (beyond the original two doubts) that makes it easier to be lenient about entirely, which is not the case with wool.

paragraphs: It is permitted to place the tzitzit on the tallit and tie them at night on a tallit designated for the day, even though according to the Rambam and those who agree with him, a day garment is exempt at night. There is no concern here of 'it must be made [for the mitzvah], not the result of something already made,' because the time [of obligation] comes on its own; and this is not comparable to a garment of only three corners, which is not obligated at all and is not fit for tzitzit at all, as mentioned in Mishb'tzot Zahav, siman 18, se'if katan 1.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to hang and tie new tzitzit on a tallit designated for the day, even if this is done at night. According to the opinion of the Rambam and those who agree with him, that a day garment is exempt from tzitzit at night, there is no problem here of 'it must be made [for the mitzvah], not the result of something already made' (meaning, there is no concern that the tallit would be considered as having already become obligated in tzitzit in an invalid manner, requiring it to be redone), because the obligation will arrive on its own once the day comes. This differs from the case of a garment with only three corners, which is not obligated at all and is not fit for the mitzvah of tzitzit at all.
takeaways: It is permitted to place tzitzit on a day-tallit even at nighttime — there is no problem of 'it must be made, not the result of something already made,' since the obligation will arrive on its own once the day comes.

paragraphs: The tzitzit are accessories of the mitzvah (tashmishei mitzvah) and have no inherent sanctity in themselves. Therefore, while they are fixed on the tallit, it is forbidden to use them for a mundane purpose, such as tying something with them and the like. One should also be careful that they not be dragged along the ground, because of disgracing the mitzvah. After they have been detached from the tallit, one may discard them, only he should not throw them into the garbage or a disgraceful place; and there are those who are stringent to bury them [in a respectful manner], and blessing will come upon them [for doing so].

clarification.explanation: The threads of the tzitzit themselves are considered 'accessories of a mitzvah' (objects used for the purpose of a mitzvah) and have no inherent sanctity of their own. Therefore, as long as they are fixed on the tallit, it is forbidden to use them for mundane purposes, such as tying something with them. One should also be careful that they not be dragged along the floor, out of respect for the mitzvah ('disgracing the mitzvah'). After the tzitzit have become detached from the tallit, it is permitted to discard them, but not to a disgraceful place such as the garbage. Some are stringent to bury them [in a respectful manner], and it is proper to act this way.
takeaways: It is forbidden to use tzitzit attached to a tallit for mundane purposes, and they should not be dragged along the ground, out of respect for the mitzvah.
After they become detached from the tallit, it is permitted to discard them in a clean place; some have the custom of burying them.

paragraphs: Tallitot used for the mitzvah that have worn out — it is forbidden to wipe with them or to put them to a disgraceful use, but rather one should discard them, and they wear out on their own. And those that people are accustomed to throw away in the synagogue, and the sextons wipe the synagogue's candles with them, and also wipe their hands that are dirtied by this oil — this is called a disgraceful use and is forbidden.

clarification.explanation: Tallitot used for the mitzvah that have worn out (become completely threadbare) — it is forbidden to use them for wiping or for any other disgraceful use; one should only discard them, since they are 'vessels that become invalid of their own accord' (items that wear out and become disqualified by themselves). Rabbi Yosef Chaim notes that nevertheless there are places where it is customary to throw them away in the synagogue, and the sextons use them to clean the synagogue's candles or to wipe their hands that have been dirtied by this oil — and this is a disgraceful use and is forbidden.
takeaways: Worn-out tallitot should be discarded, not used for cleaning or any other disgraceful purpose — this is actually forbidden, even if mistakenly practiced.

paragraphs: It is permitted to make a small tallit out of a large piece of cloth, so concluded the Rabbi Beit Yehuda, siman 29. But the Rabbi Lev Chaim, of blessed memory, siman 92, expressed doubt about this, since according to the mystical tradition, a large tallit has a great advantage over a small tallit — and the truth is with him regarding this. However, if part of it has worn out and is no longer fit to be worn [as a large tallit], one may make a small tallit from the sturdy part that remains, and there is no concern about this at all.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to cut from a large tallit and make from it a small tallit, as the Rabbi Beit Yehuda concluded. However, the Rabbi Lev Chaim expresses doubt about this, on the grounds that according to the mystical tradition, a large tallit has a greater spiritual advantage than a small tallit — and in this he is correct. Nevertheless, if the large tallit has already partly worn out and is no longer fit to be worn as a large tallit, it is permitted to take the sturdy part that remains and make from it a small tallit, and there is no concern about this at all.
takeaways: A large tallit that has partly worn out — it is permitted to make a small tallit from its sturdy remaining part.
A whole and intact large tallit — it is preferable not to cut it down into a small tallit, because of its superior spiritual advantage.
